title: What a great eCommerce checkout page looks like in the UAE
summary: Learn how to set up your checkout page for your e-commerce store and how to improve conversions & reduce cart abandonment with 4 key strategies.

## How to set up a checkout page for your eCommerce store


Every online store works a bit differently, so the exact setup depends on how your store was built.


But no matter where you’re starting from, a great checkout page starts with three core steps that make it easier for customers to convert:


### Decide if your customers will use a hosted or embedded checkout to complete their payment


This choice shapes what customers see after they’re ready to pay and can narrow down which


[payment gateways](https://ziina.com/blog/top-payment-gateways-UAE) will work for your online store.


A hosted checkout sends your customer to a new tab when it's time to pay. They land on a secure page managed by your payment gateway provider and complete the payment there.


Since the payment gateway provider is responsible for the payment page, there's less to customize and fewer decisions to make about the actual payment form.


An embedded checkout, on the other hand, keeps the secure payment form inside your own store's website. The customer can enter their card details or choose a digital wallet without moving to another page, so they stay within your branded online store experience from the moment they land on your site until the moment they pay.


This approach keeps your checkout consistent and on-brand, but you'll need a payment gateway that supports embedded checkout for your specific store setup.


When you're comparing


[payment gateways](https://ziina.com/payment-gateway) , check:


- If the provider works with your exact eCommerce platform or custom website


- Whether it offers hosted checkout, embedded checkout, or both through that integration


- If setup requires a ready-made plugin, help from a developer, or a custom API integration


It also matters which credit cards, digital wallets, currencies, and checkout languages the integration supports.


### Configure the checkout form to be as easy as possible for customers


Once you’ve added your payment gateway, take a closer look at the checkout form itself.


Open the checkout editor in your platform or give your web developer a clear layout plan. Review every field on your form and decide what customers really need to enter at each stage.


The main job of your checkout is to clearly display the key order details with minimal distractions:


- Show item images, quantities, individual prices, and ideally, allow customers to make changes to their order right in the cart.


- Let shoppers select local delivery, express shipping, or physical store pickup.


- Calculate shipping fees, promotional discounts, and custom charges automatically.


- If your business is registered for VAT, set your checkout to add the standard


[5% UAE VAT](https://tax.gov.ae/en/services/vat.registration.aspx) and make sure customers can see it in the total price before they pay.


- A clear error message should pop up if customers miss a required field or enter info in the wrong format.


- Customers should see an official order confirmation once they’ve successfully completed their payment.


The way you arrange your form fields matters just as much. For a single-page checkout, organize fields in a logical, step-by-step sequence. If you choose a multi-page setup, add progress indicators like breadcrumbs or a progress bar so shoppers always know how many steps are left.


The goal is for customers to check out with as little friction as possible while remaining secure.


With that in mind, you might also want to add a


guest checkout option


. Support for that is up to your eCommerce platform or your developer, but it’s worth looking into – and you can always set up post-purchase emails to invite customers to create an account after their purchase.


### Test the entire checkout before publishing it


Place at least one real test order on both a computer and mobile before opening your store to real customers.


In practice, that means going through the checkout process using every available payment method, delivery option, discount code, and relevant customer location. Confirm that prices and taxes update correctly, required fields behave as expected, and customers see the right confirmation after their payment goes through.


You should also test your checkout page on a range of screen sizes and keep an eye out for what happens if a customer:


- Enters incomplete or invalid information


- Tries to use an expired or declined card


- Refreshes the page or presses the back button


- Leaves checkout and returns later


Some payment gateway providers offer a test mode so you can run a few transactions without moving real money around.


For example, if you use


[Ziina's WooCommerce plugin](https://ziina.com/help-center/7908114-how-do-i-use-test-mode-in-woo-commerce) , you can toggle on Test Mode to make sure everything functions smoothly before launch.


Once everything works as expected, you can publish the checkout. As real orders roll in, you’ll likely keep finding more ways to remove friction and turn more of those visits into completed sales.


Speaking of which…


## 4 ways to improve your eCommerce checkout conversion rate


A checkout page can look great on the surface and function perfectly behind the scenes – but still lead to cart abandonment if extra fees come as a surprise, the form fields feel exhausting, or the payment step looks unfamiliar.


Here are four practical ways to make your checkout flow easier for your customers to understand and complete:


### 1. Find out where customers are dropping off before you test any changes


There’s no need to tweak your checkout layout based on guesswork. Start by figuring out the exact payment step where customers tend to abandon the purchase.


If you use a platform like Shopify or WooCommerce, check the built-in checkout funnel reports. For custom websites, have your developer set up event tracking in tools like Google Analytics to measure each stage of the buying process.


No matter which analytics you use, you’ll want to track four main milestones:


When customers…


- Start checkout


- Submit their shipping address and contact information


- Reach the payment screen


- Complete the purchase successfully


The biggest drop between two stages tells you where to investigate.


If customers leave before payment, look at the form to see if the delivery options or the way the total price is displayed could be causing hesitation.


If they leave on the payment screen, check your payment gateway logs to see if transactions are failing – if the logs look okay, your customers could be backing out due to something else on the front end, like not seeing their preferred payment method.


Once you have a likely explanation, test one change aimed at that problem. Then compare completed orders before and after the test.


Based on your findings, you might decide to…


### 2. Show the full price as early as you can


Seeing a new charge near the end of checkout can make customers think twice about the order. So, try to display shipping fees, estimated taxes, and any handling charges as early in the process as possible.


If shipping costs depend on the delivery address, add a note in the cart stating that delivery is calculated at checkout. As soon as the user enters their city or area, update the final total.


To make address entry more seamless for your customers – and reduce typing across devices – you could also add autofill and address lookup to your checkout form, depending on your setup.


On mobile devices, keep the total price summary visible or easily expandable with a single tap. Shoppers shouldn’t have to leave the checkout experience to double-check what they’ve entered or confirm how much they’re about to pay.


### 3. For each part of your checkout experience, ask yourself: “Do I really need it?”


The last thing you want is for the checkout form to slow customers down right when they’re ready to pay. To speed up the checkout flow, go through every field and make sure you really need each answer to complete the order.


Often, a question like “How did you hear about us?” can wait – so it’s best to save marketing questions for post-purchase emails or order confirmation pages.


Your checkout structure should also make sense with what you sell:


- Single-page checkouts


work well for straightforward orders with fewer choices, but they’re not always the best move for more complex purchases where customers have to schedule a delivery window or choose other add-ons.


- Multi-page checkouts


can keep the checkout sections visually clean for those more complex orders, but you’ll need to include a progress indicator and ensure customers can go back without losing info they’ve already entered to keep the experience low-friction.


No part of your checkout experience should feel like a hurdle. And that brings us to the final payment step…


### 4. Include the most common payment methods based on region and keep the page on-brand


For customers to confidently enter their sensitive payment details, the payment step of your checkout experience needs to feel secure, convenient, and recognizably on-brand.


That starts with your payment methods. UAE customers will expect to see major cards and familiar digital wallets like


[Apple Pay](https://ziina.com/blog/apple-pay-integration-on-website) and Google Pay, so make sure those are available and easy to spot at a glance.


If you offer multiple payment options, the wording around each one matters, too. Customers should understand who is actually processing the payment no matter which payment method they choose.


For example, Ziina’s WooCommerce plugin lets merchants change the title and description customers see next to the Ziina payment option. You can use that space to clarify their options, like “pay by card via Ziina Pay” instead of leaving them guessing.
